content: Recent rainfall in the upper districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has led to a noticeable increase in water inflow at Tarbela Dam, said the dam authorities on Thursday. Dam officials said that the water level in Tarbela Dam has risen to 1,451 feet, which is 49 feet above the dead level of 1,402 feet. The dam’s maximum level is 1,550 feet. The inflow of water into the dam has been recorded at 36,500 cusecs, while the outflow stands at 15,000 cusecs, indicating a steady accumulation of water due to the recent rains. Despite the improved water situation, power generation remains limited. Out of the dam’s 17 power generation units, only 4 units are currently operational, while 13 units are shut down. The total electricity generation capacity of Tarbela Dam is 4,988 megawatts, but currently, only 760 megawatts of electricity is being produced. Authorities have attributed the rising water levels to the recent rainfall in the upper regions of the province, which has positively impacted the reservoir levels. Further updates are expected as weather conditions evolve and water inflow continues to change, they said.
title: Water inflow rises at Tarbela Dam after recent rains - Daily Times

content: The Tarbela 5th Extension Hydropower Project (T5) has achieved a significant milestone in WAPDA’s engagement with international carbon markets. The Project is expected to reduce approximately 565,905 tons of CO? emissions annually, contributing to a total reduction of 5,659,053 tons over a fixed 10-year crediting period. The verification process for the Project has commenced and, upon completion, the Project will be registered with the Global Carbon Council (GCC). This will make T5 Pakistan’s first hydropower project to achieve GCC registration. The progress has been made possible with technical support from the World Bank and through the successful completion of key milestones, including project submission and the engagement of GCC-approved international verifier namely LGAI Technologies, Spain. As part of the verification process, a site visit was conducted by the local auditor of LGAI Technologies. During the visit, GM/PD T5, Umair Manan, briefed the auditor on the overall progress of the Project. Director (Civil) T5, Faisal Hayat, and Assistant Director Environment T5, Asima Mughal, also informed the auditor about ongoing construction activities, in addition to environmental and social management aspects of the Project. The auditor appreciated the progress achieved across various components of the Project and expressed satisfaction with compliance to environmental and social plans. The Tarbela 5th Extension Hydropower Project, on completion, will play a vital role in promoting clean energy and supporting Pakistan’s commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
title: Tarbela 5th extension advances towards carbon market registration - Daily Times

content: The federal government has appointed Shafquat Hussain Wadho as Member Sindh in the Indus River System Authority (IRSA) for a period of three years. According to an official notification, the government also accepted the resignation of Muhammad Ehsan ul Haq Leghari from the post of Member IRSA Sindh with effect from May 6, 2026 in terms of Section 4(5) of the IRSA Act, 1992, it further said.
title: Govt appoints Shafquat Hussain Wadho as IRSA member from Sindh - Daily Times

content: Water and Power Development Authority has revealed that Tarbela Dam supplied 586 billion units of low-cost electricity and released more than 419 million acre-feet of water for irrigation during the last 50 years. According to Wapda, the mega hydropower project generated economic benefits worth nearly $460 billion for Pakistan since beginning operations in 1974. Officials described the dam as one of the country’s most important national infrastructure projects supporting energy production, agriculture, and economic development simultaneously. The details were shared during a visit by Wapda Chairman Muhammad Saeed to the Tarbela Dam and Khanpur Dam extension projects currently under construction. During the visit, the chairman reviewed progress on the Tarbela Fifth Extension Hydropower Project and also witnessed testing and commissioning activities at the Tarbela Fourth Extension Project. Senior officials from the Indus River System Authority and members of Irsa’s technical committee accompanied him throughout the inspection process. Read more : WAPDA chief reviews progress on Tarbela’s fifth extension project Officials briefed the chairman on ongoing work related to the intake structure, tunnels, penstock systems, powerhouse construction, tailrace canal, and switchyard infrastructure at the fifth extension project. They informed the chairman that construction activities were progressing steadily and all major components were expected to be completed within the planned schedule. Muhammad Saeed directed contractors, engineers, and consultants to accelerate development work further while maintaining strict quality control measures and international safety standards during construction activities. The Tarbela Fifth Extension Hydropower Project will add 1,530 megawatts of electricity generation capacity to Pakistan’s national grid once completed successfully. The project is being financed with support from the World Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, which are contributing $390 million and $300 million respectively. Following completion, Tarbela Dam’s total installed electricity generation capacity will increase significantly from 4,888 megawatts to approximately 6,418 megawatts, strengthening Pakistan’s energy production capabilities. Read more : WB directors brifed on Tarbela Dam’s extension Meanwhile, officials also briefed the chairman about the performance of the Tarbela Fourth Extension Project, which started electricity generation operations in March 2018 with financial assistance from the World Bank. According to Wapda, the facility has already supplied more than 33.254 billion units of electricity to the national grid since becoming operational. Authorities additionally conducted testing and commissioning of the low-level outlet system to ensure adequate water releases during the upcoming kharif agricultural season across Pakistan. Energy experts believe Tarbela Dam continues playing a critical role in supporting Pakistan’s agricultural irrigation network while also providing affordable electricity for households, industries, and commercial activities nationwide. Officials noted that expanding hydropower capacity remains essential for reducing dependence on costly imported fuels and improving long-term energy security. Consequently, the government is accelerating major hydroelectric projects to meet rising electricity demand, stabilise energy supplies, and strengthen economic growth across the country in coming years.
title: Tarbela Dam powers Pakistan with massive 50-year contribution - Daily Times

content: Sindh continues to face a significant water shortage as the Indus River System Authority (Irsa) has decided to maintain its policy of equalising water shortages between Punjab and Sindh despite objections from the provincial government. Read More: IRSA rejects Sindh’s less water supply claim According to irrigation officials, Sindh has been experiencing an overall water shortage of 22 per cent for the past ten days. The province has formally raised concerns over Irsa’s decision, arguing that excess water received during unusual rainfall events earlier this year should not be deducted from its share under the 1991 Water Apportionment Accord. Irsa Director Operations Khalid Idrees Rana said the authority is adjusting water use and working to equalise shortages between the two provinces until June 10. He noted that river flows remain unsatisfactory compared to the same period last year, although rising temperatures could improve water availability through increased snowmelt in the coming weeks. Sindh officials maintain that exceptional rainfall in April led to unusually high inflows in the Indus River system, particularly from the Kabul River. They argue that the surplus water was generated by natural conditions and should be treated similarly to flood flows that were shared by provinces in previous years rather than being counted against Sindh’s allocated share. Irsa, however, has yet to make a final decision on Sindh’s representation. The authority points to significantly lower water inflows at major reservoirs, including Tarbela and Mangla dams, compared to last year. Current inflow figures are considerably below those recorded during the same period in 2025, contributing to the overall shortage across the system. The shortage has affected irrigation supplies throughout Sindh. Guddu Barrage recorded a 42pc shortfall, while Kotri and Sukkur barrages reported shortages of 29pc and 11pc respectively. Several major canals, particularly those serving rice-growing areas, are receiving reduced supplies as the sowing season begins. Read More: Irsa Blocks Plan to Drain Half of Tarbela Dam Water Level Farmers and irrigation experts have also expressed concern over continued water withdrawals through inter-provincial link canals, arguing that the reduced river flows are placing additional pressure on Sindh’s agricultural sector and water resources.
title: Sindh faces water shortage as Irsa maintains allocation policy - Daily Times

content: A high-level delegation of the World Bank, led by its Country Director for Pakistan, Bolorma Amgaabazar, visited the under-construction Tarbela Fifth Extension Hydropower Project (T-5) and expressed satisfaction over the pace and quality of work being carried out on the strategic energy project. During the two-day visit, the delegation was given a comprehensive briefing on the project’s construction activities, technical progress, financial management and social development initiatives aimed at improving the welfare of local communities. The delegation also inspected various construction sites and reviewed ongoing engineering works. The World Bank team appreciated the operational performance of the 1,410-megawatt Tarbela Fourth Extension Hydropower Project, highlighting its contribution to the national power system through the generation of clean and affordable electricity. Expressing confidence in the project’s advancement, the delegation reaffirmed the World Bank’s commitment to maintaining its strong development partnership with the Water and Power Development Authority (WAPDA) to support Pakistan’s efforts in expanding renewable energy generation and ensuring the supply of reliable, low-cost and environmentally sustainable hydropower to the national grid. Officials informed the delegation about the project’s implementation status and future milestones, while also outlining measures being taken to ensure timely completion and compliance with international standards. Among those present during the visit were WAPDA Member (Finance) Naveed Asghar Chaudhry, Member (Power) Muhammad Irfan, General Manager/Project Director T-5 Umair Manan, General Manager/Project Director Tarbela Dam Project Anwar Shah, Advisor T-4 and T-5 Azam Joiya, Advisor Tarbela Dam Project Hazrat Umar and other senior officials. At the conclusion of the visit, commemorative souvenirs were presented to the members of the World Bank delegation in recognition of their continued support for Pakistan’s hydropower development initiatives.
title: WB team satisfied with progress on Fifth Tarbela extension project - Daily Times

content: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) on Friday warned of rising water levels in the Indus River after the spillways of Tarbela Dam were opened due to increased inflows caused by rapid glacier melt and rainfall in upper catchment areas. The move is expected to increase water discharge downstream, posing risks to low lying areas, particularly in Layyah, Bhakkar and Mianwali, prompting authorities to urge residents and tourists to stay away from the river and water channels. NDMA said the rise in river flows was driven by increasing temperatures that have accelerated glacier melt, coupled with rainfall in northern parts of the country. The opening of Tarbela Dam’s spillways is part of efforts to safely manage water levels at the reservoir. The authority cautioned that water levels and flow in downstream areas of the Indus River may rise significantly. Residents living near the riverbanks have been advised to remain vigilant and strictly follow instructions issued by local administrations. Tourists have been urged to avoid recreational activities in and around the Indus River during this period, while the public has been advised to stay away from water channels and river crossings experiencing strong currents. NDMA said it is continuously monitoring the evolving situation through its National Emergencies Operation Center and ensuring timely dissemination of risk assessments and advisories to relevant institutions and the public to minimise potential hazards.
title: Tarbela spillways opened as Indus River flow surges: NDMA - Daily Times

content: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) on Saturday warned of rising water flows in major rivers and the risk of low to moderate-level flooding across several parts of the country on August 8-9, as its National Emergencies Operation Centre (NEOC) reviewed river flows, reservoir levels and emerging monsoon risks and directed local administrations to pre-position resources and keep evacuation arrangements ready in vulnerable areas. According to the NEOC assessment, low-level flooding is currently being observed in the Indus River at Kalabagh, Chashma, Taunsa and Guddu. Flows in the Ravi, Chenab, Jhelum, Kabul and Sutlej rivers, as well as hill torrents in Dera Ghazi Khan and Rajanpur and Nullah Lai, remain normal. The NDMA said water flows in major rivers are expected to increase on August 8 and 9. Low-level flows are likely at Kalabagh, Chashma, Taunsa, Guddu and Sukkur on the Indus, Marala on the Chenab and Balloki on the Ravi. Low-level flows are also expected in the Jhelum and downstream areas of Mangla Dam, adjoining rivers and at Adezai on the Kabul River. The authority warned of low to moderate-level flooding in streams and nullahs in Chitral, Upper Dir, Abbottabad, Shangla, Khyber, Orakzai, Kohat, Tank and North and South Waziristan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In Azad Kashmir, Bagh and Kotli face the risk of sudden low to moderate-level flooding, while similar risks have been identified in Zhob, Musakhel, Kohlu, Barkhan and Dera Bugti in Balochistan. In Punjab, hill torrents in Dera Ghazi Khan and Rajanpur could experience low to moderate flooding. Urban flooding is also possible in Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, Sialkot, Narowal, Faisalabad, Okara and Lahore. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) on Saturday reported that water storage at Tarbela and Mangla dams remained high amid the ongoing monsoon season, with Tarbela holding 97.94 per cent of its storage capacity and Mangla 62.99pc, as the authority reviewed reservoir levels to assess the country’s water and flood situation and support timely preparedness measures. According to the latest assessment by the NDMA’s National Emergencies Operation Centre (NEOC), the water level at Tarbela Dam stood at 1,548 feet, with storage recorded at 97.94pc. The corresponding storage level during the same period last year was 95.98pc. At Mangla Dam, the water level was recorded at 1,205.2 feet, with storage at 62.99pc, compared with 62.80pc during the same period last year. The latest figures were came as the monsoon season was continuing to bring increased rainfall and rising water flows across parts of the country. The NDMA is maintaining close monitoring of reservoir levels and river flows and providing timely information and alerts to relevant authorities to strengthen preparedness against potential flooding.
title: River flows, flash flood risk rise across Pakistan, warns NDMA - Daily Times

content: The National Disaster Management Authority has warned of rising water flows in major rivers during August 8 and 9, with low-level flooding already reported at several Indus River locations. The National Emergencies Operation Centre said low-level flooding was recorded at Kalabagh, Chashma, Taunsa and Guddu. Meanwhile, water levels in the Ravi, Chenab, Jhelum, Kabul and Sutlej remained within normal ranges. Authorities are monitoring river flows and dam storage as monsoon activity continues across the country. Read more : Field Marshal Asim Munir visits NDMA emergency centre The NDMA expects low-level flooding at Kalabagh, Chashma, Taunsa, Guddu and Sukkur along the Indus, while Marala on the Chenab and Baloki on the Ravi could also experience increased flows. Low-level water flow is also possible in upper Jhelum areas and around Mangla Dam, while Adizai on the Kabul River could face similar conditions. The authority has urged local administrations to prepare resources and evacuation arrangements in vulnerable areas. Several regions face additional risks from heavy rainfall, flash floods and overflowing storm drains during the current monsoon period. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, low to medium flooding is possible in Chitral, Upper Dir, Abbottabad, Shangla, Khyber, Orakzai, Kohat, Tank and North and South Waziristan. Bagh and Kotli in Azad Kashmir, along with Zhob, Musakhel, Kohlu, Barkhan and Dera Bugti in Balochistan, also face flash flood risks. Read more : NDMA warns of rising flood threat across Pakistan – In Punjab, authorities have identified low to medium flood risks in urban areas including Rawalpindi, Gujranwala, Sialkot, Narowal, Faisalabad, Okara and Lahore. Mountain rain drains in DG Khan and Rajanpur also remain areas of concern during heavy rainfall. The NDMA has advised administrations to move emergency resources to sensitive locations before conditions worsen. It has also called for safe evacuation arrangements to protect communities in vulnerable areas. Water storage at the country’s major dams remains high, adding importance to continued monitoring of incoming river flows. Tarbela Dam’s water level stood at 1,548 feet, with storage reaching 97.94 percent, compared with 95.98 percent during the same period last year. Mangla Dam recorded a water level of 1,205.2 feet and storage of 62.99 percent, slightly above the 62.80 percent recorded last year. These levels require authorities to closely monitor further inflows. The NDMA has urged residents, tourists and travellers to stay away from rivers, drains, flooded roads and fast-moving water during the monsoon. People should never attempt to cross floodwater on foot or by vehicle because even shallow, rapidly moving water can sweep away people and vehicles. Mountainous areas also face increased risks of landslides, debris flows and sudden flash floods, particularly after heavy rainfall. Authorities have advised the public to check weather forecasts and road conditions before travelling and avoid unnecessary journeys during severe weather. People should follow official instructions, avoid roads closed by administrations and take immediate precautions when alerts are issued. The NDMA is continuing to provide updates to relevant agencies and has encouraged citizens to use the official Pak NDMA Disaster Alert app for timely warnings and emergency information.
title: NDMA warns of rising river flows and flood risks across Pakistan - Daily Times

content: Tarbela Dam has reached its maximum storage capacity after heavy monsoon rains, while rising river levels have increased flood risks across several parts of Pakistan. Low-level flooding has been reported in the Indus River at Tarbela, Kalabagh, Chashma and Taunsa, while Mangla Dam has reached around 68% of its storage capacity. Read more : Tarbela Dam powers Pakistan with massive 50-year contribution Authorities expect low-level flooding in the Ravi and Chenab rivers within the next 24 to 48 hours, while medium-level flooding could affect connected streams and nullahs from August 17 to 19. The weather department has forecast widespread heavy rainfall across Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Islamabad and Kashmir during the next 48 hours, increasing pressure on rivers and drainage systems. Read more : WAPDA chief reviews progress on Tarbela’s fifth extension project Heavy rain is also expected in upper catchment areas of the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi and Sutlej rivers, while thunderstorms may affect Rawalpindi, Lahore, Gujranwala, Sialkot and surrounding districts. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, authorities have been alerted to heavy rainfall in Peshawar, Mardan, Swat, Abbottabad and Haripur, while upper Indus areas and parts of Balochistan may also receive rain. Meanwhile, Gilgit-Baltistan districts including Astore, Diamer, Gilgit and Skardu are likely to experience thunderstorms, prompting authorities across vulnerable areas to remain alert and take precautionary measures.
title: Tarbela Dam reaches full capacity as flood risk rises - Daily Times

content: Indus River System Authority (IRSA) on Sunday released 173,800 cusecs of water from various rim stations with an inflow of 109,000 cusecs. According to the data released by IRSA, the water level in the River Indus at Tarbela Dam stood at 1527.19 feet, which was 125.19 feet higher than the dead level of 1402.00 feet. Water inflow and outflow in the dam were recorded as 65,000 cusecs and 100,000 cusecs, respectively. The water level in the Jhelum River at Mangla Dam was 1213.85 feet, which was 163.85 feet higher than its dead level of 1,050 feet. The inflow and outflow of water were recorded as 9,200 cusecs and 39,000 cusecs, respectively. The release of water at Kalabagh, Taunsa, Guddu, and Sukkur was recorded as 106,700, 104,500, 94,300, and 42,300 cusecs, respectively. Similarly, from River Kabul, a total of 14,000 cusecs of water was released at Nowshera, and 7,000 cusecs were released from River Chenab at Marala.
title: IRSA releases 173,800 cusecs water - Daily Times
